papers.title: Bio-PM-Guided Synthetic IMU Generation
papers.authors: Deepali Singh, Deepesh Parpani, Aviral Gupta
papers.what: Collecting and labeling inertial measurement unit (IMU) data for human activity recognition (HAR) is expensive, and models trained on one group of subjects often fail to generalize to unseen individuals. papers.summary: Collecting and labeling inertial measurement unit (IMU) data for human activity recognition (HAR) is expensive, and models trained on one group of subjects often fail to generalize to unseen individuals. Even with balanced data, classifiers struggle to distinguish dynamically similar activity classes and benefit from targeted augmentation. We explore whether synthetic IMU data generated in the representation space of a pretrained biosignal encoder, Bio-PM \cite{b1}, can serve as a practical augmentation source. Rather than synthesizing raw signals, we leverage Bio-PM's frozen encoder to convert 10-second IMU windows into token embedding sequences and train class-conditional decoders in this space: (1) an autoregressive transformer decoder that predicts tokens sequentially, and (2) a diffusion decoder that learns the token distribution through a denoising objective. We analyze generation realism through distributional metrics and embedding-space visualizations, evaluate downstream utility through leave-one-subject-out HAR classification, and present a PatchDecoder for approximate raw waveform reconstruction. Our diffusion decoder achieves a Train-on-Synthetic-Test-on-Real (TSTR) macro-F1 of 0.68, demonstrating that generated tokens are realistic enough to train a classifier that transfers to real data. Combining synthetic-token augmentation with a 320-dimensional gravity-aware feature representation raises LOSO macro-F1 from 0.729 to 0.809 over a real-only baseline across 51 subjects on the WISDM benchmark, with statistically significant gains concentrated in the most challenging activity classes. These results demonstrate that high-fidelity generation in a pretrained encoder's representation space is achievable and practically useful for cross-subject HAR augmentation.

papers.title: Text-Aware, Vision-Blind: How Multimodal Image Editing Systems Handle Unsafe Inputs
papers.authors: Ziqing Yang, Yixin Wu, Michael Backes, Yang Zhang
papers.what: Multimodal image generation systems have made rapid progress and increasingly emphasize content safety. papers.summary: Multimodal image generation systems have made rapid progress and increasingly emphasize content safety. However, their safety mechanisms tend to rely on a single modality and lack joint consideration of both visual content and text prompts, particularly in instruction-guided image editing, where the uploaded image may itself carry risk. We thus introduce EditSafetyBench, a benchmark that measures system-level safety awareness of advanced image editing systems, containing 5,940 image-instruction pairs, covering safe and unsafe images across 11 risk categories and three edit intents. We then probe the benchmark dataset on four systems, including Gemini, GPT, Qwen API, and Qwen Local. Based on our evaluation, we observe a systematic text-vision safety mismatch: Gemini and GPT refuse 87.1\% and 81.6\% cases containing unsafe-intent editing prompts, while only refusing 24.2\% and 22.4\% cases with both unsafe images and neutral instructions. At the category level, most risks are considered inconsistently by different systems, e.g., GPT allows 70.4\% editing attempts of unsafe political content while Gemini only allows 34.8\%. Notably, sexual content shows the strongest visual sensitivity, likely benefiting from mature NSFW identification works. Our findings highlight the need for safety guardrails that jointly reason over both visual and textual modalities in image editing systems.

papers.title: One Prior, Two Dynamics: Repurposing Video Diffusion Transformers for Self-Supervised Latent Action Learning
papers.authors: Yuxin Jiang, Wenqiang Sun, Jiaqi Li, Yuchao Gu et al.
papers.what: Videos reveal how the world changes, but rarely the actions that cause those changes. Latent action learning recovers such supervision from visual transitions, yet often learns the underlying dynamics largely from scratch. We ask whether a pretrained video generator can instead provide the prior for
papers.summary: Videos reveal how the world changes, but rarely the actions that cause those changes. Latent action learning recovers such supervision from visual transitions, yet often learns the underlying dynamics largely from scratch. We ask whether a pretrained video generator can instead provide the prior for both inverse and forward dynamics. We introduce O$^{2}$LaF, built on a simple principle: one prior, two dynamics. We initialize both models from the same pretrained video DiT and adapt them to their distinct roles: a feed-forward transition encoder with learnable action queries for inverse dynamics, and a causal, action-conditioned video generator for forward dynamics. By controlling information access and optimizing both dynamics end-to-end through a compact bottleneck, O$^{2}$LaF learns transferable actions from unlabeled videos. Across navigation and robotic manipulation, O$^{2}$LaF sets a new state of the art in few-shot action probing and enables stronger zero-shot action transfer across visual contexts and embodiments. Beyond generative video priors, we further extend our framework to predictive representation priors such as V-JEPA2, achieving competitive performance. Our findings suggest a broader paradigm for latent-action learning: repurposing pretrained video models to discover transferable actions and predict their consequences.

papers.authors: Adrià Ciurana Lanau, Harleen Hanspal, Lusine Abrahamyan, Emilio Tylson Baixauli et al.

papers.summary: Graphic designs are ordered compositions of RGBA layers whose separation enables selection, movement, and reuse. Existing layered models represent each layer with a full-canvas or region-sized spatial latent grid, so representation size grows with the cumulative spatial extent of the layers. We present ProtoDiffusion, a latent-diffusion framework built on ProtoVAE, a multi-layer variational autoencoder that encodes a design into one shared spatial prototype and one candidate vector per layer. Each candidate conditions a shared decoder to reconstruct its corresponding RGBA layer. For $N$ layers, the representation contains $HW+N$ tokens before backbone-specific packing, compared with $NHW$ for full-grid-per-layer representations. ProtoDiffusion jointly denoises the prototype and a fixed set of candidate slots, conditioned on an image or text, with bounding boxes as optional layout guidance. The model leaves unneeded slots empty and determines the number of layers and, in absence of boxes, their layout, requiring neither as input. The same architecture supports both image-to-design and text-to-design. ProtoVAE achieves high-fidelity reconstruction from its compact shared latent representation, reaching 40.43 dB PSNR on layer crops. On the LayerD evaluation split, image-to-design achieves RGB L1 scores of 0.040 with bounding boxes and 0.057 without, with box-guided alpha soft IoU (0.850) comparable to the strongest fine-tuned baseline (0.871). On merged images, text-to-design reaches 66.41 FID versus 86.84 for FLUX.2 [klein], achieves a 0.860 text-accuracy score, and runs $19.1\times$ faster than the same-backbone generation-then-decomposition cascade.

papers.title: Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
papers.authors: Snell, Charlie, Lee, Jaehoon, Kelvin Xu, Aviral Kumar
papers.what: [Conference] Enabling LLMs to improve their outputs by using more test-time computation is a critical step towards building generally self-improving agents that can operate on open-ended natural language. In this paper, we study the scaling of inference-time computation in LLMs, with a focus
papers.summary: Enabling LLMs to improve their outputs by using more test-time computation is a critical step towards building generally self-improving agents that can operate on open-ended natural language. In this paper, we study the scaling of inference-time computation in LLMs, with a focus on answering the question: if an LLM is allowed to use a fixed but non-trivial amount of inference-time compute, how much can it improve its performance on a challenging prompt? Answering this question has implications not only on the achievable performance of LLMs, but also on the future of LLM pretraining and how one should tradeoff inference-time and pre-training compute. Despite its importance, little research attempted to understand the scaling behaviors of various test-time inference methods. Moreover, current work largely provides negative results for a number of these strategies. In this work, we analyze two primary mechanisms to scale test-time computation: (1) searching against dense, process-based verifier reward models; and (2) updating the model's distribution over a response adaptively, given the prompt at test time. We find that in both cases, the effectiveness of different approaches to scaling test-time compute critically varies depending on the difficulty of the prompt. This observation motivates applying a "compute-optimal" scaling strategy, which acts to most effectively allocate test-time compute adaptively per prompt. Using this compute-optimal strategy, we can improve the efficiency of test-time compute scaling by more than 4x compared to a best-of-N baseline. Additionally, in a FLOPs-matched evaluation, we find that on problems where a smaller base model attains somewhat non-trivial success rates, test-time compute can be used to outperform a 14x larger model.

papers.title: GSM-Symbolic: Understanding the Limitations of Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.authors: Iman Mirzadeh, Keivan Alizadeh, Hooman Shahrokhi, Oncel Tuzel et al.
papers.what: [Conference] Recent advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs) have sparked interest in their formal reasoning capabilities, particularly in mathematics. The GSM8K benchmark is widely used to assess the mathematical reasoning of models on grade-school-level questions. While the performance
papers.summary: Recent advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs) have sparked interest in their formal reasoning capabilities, particularly in mathematics. The GSM8K benchmark is widely used to assess the mathematical reasoning of models on grade-school-level questions. While the performance of LLMs on GSM8K has significantly improved in recent years, it remains unclear whether their mathematical reasoning capabilities have genuinely advanced, raising questions about the reliability of the reported metrics. To address these concerns, we conduct a large-scale study on several SOTA open and closed models. To overcome the limitations of existing evaluations, we introduce GSM-Symbolic, an improved benchmark created from symbolic templates that allow for the generation of a diverse set of questions. GSM-Symbolic enables more controllable evaluations, providing key insights and more reliable metrics for measuring the reasoning capabilities of models.Our findings reveal that LLMs exhibit noticeable variance when responding to different instantiations of the same question. Specifically, the performance of all models declines when only the numerical values in the question are altered in the GSM-Symbolic benchmark. Furthermore, we investigate the fragility of mathematical reasoning in these models and show that their performance significantly deteriorates as the number of clauses in a question increases. We hypothesize that this decline is because current LLMs cannot perform genuine logical reasoning; they replicate reasoning steps from their training data. Adding a single clause that seems relevant to the question causes significant performance drops (up to 65%) across all state-of-the-art models, even though the clause doesn't contribute to the reasoning chain needed for the final answer. Overall, our work offers a more nuanced understanding of LLMs' capabilities and limitations in mathematical reasoning.

papers.title: Products of Distinguisher Hulls
papers.what: [Explore] The distinguisher hull of two distributions is the convex hull of the pairs of acceptance probabilities of tests in a specified class. We study its behavior under independent products for size-bounded Boolean circuits. We derive a geometric consequence of Dwork and Tankala's supe
papers.summary: The distinguisher hull of two distributions is the convex hull of the pairs of acceptance probabilities of tests in a specified class. We study its behavior under independent products for size-bounded Boolean circuits. We derive a geometric consequence of Dwork and Tankala's supersimulator theorem (FOCS 2026), giving a substantially different proof of approximate product containment for distinguisher hulls. In particular, our construction uses nonadaptive sampling in place of adaptive score corrections.

papers.title: Classical Oracle Separation of QMA from the QCMA Hierarchy and Quantum Cryptography Even When P = QCMA

Inspired by the Codeword-Hash Structure problem recently introduced by Cakan (arXiV, 2026) to separate $\mathsf{QMA}$ from $\mat
papers.summary: Remark: This work is in submission at STOC'27 and thus the full manuscript has been publicly posted on the conference website since November 3rd, 2026. Inspired by the Codeword-Hash Structure problem recently introduced by Cakan (arXiV, 2026) to separate $\mathsf{QMA}$ from $\mathsf{QCIP}$, we introduce a new problem called Codeword-Hash pairs in Noise ($\mathsf{CHN}$) and prove that, in the query complexity model, it is in $\mathsf{QMA}$ but hard for the $\mathsf{QCMA}$ hierarchy $\mathsf{QCMAH} = \bigcup_{d\geq1}\mathsf{QCMA}^{\mathsf{QCMA}^{\cdots^{\mathsf{QCMA}}}}$, the classical-witness quantum-verifier analogue of $\mathsf{PH}=\bigcup_{d\ge1}\mathsf{NP}^{\mathsf{NP}^{\cdots^{\mathsf{NP}}}}$. Using this problem, we show that there exists a classical oracle ${O}$ such that $\mathsf{P}^{O}=\mathsf{BQP}^{O}=\mathsf{QCMA}^{O} =\mathsf{QCMAH}^{O} \subset \mathsf{QMA}^{O} \text{ but } \mathsf{QMA}^{O}\not\subseteq\mathsf{QCMAH}^{O},$ thus showing that quantum state or quantum proof advantage could exist even if classical computers can efficiently solve any problem that can be quantumly verified with a classical proof. Further, using our problem, we show that various quantum cryptographic primitives can exist even when $\mathsf{P} = \mathsf{QCMA}$ and thus neither quantum-computable one-way functions nor (verifiable) quantum computational advantage exist. In particular, relative to a classical oracle ${O}$ with $\mathsf{P}^{O}=\mathsf{BQP}^{O}=\mathsf{QCMA}^{O}=\mathsf{QCMAH}^{O}$, there exist pseudorandom states with classical keys and public-key encryption with copy-protected quantum decryption keys and classical public keys and ciphertexts, among other primitives, answering an open question of Kretschmer, Qian, and Tal (STOC 2025).
